On 4 February 1948 Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, became independent from Britain after 133 years as a colony. Unlike India the year before, it happened without violence.

The island had been well prepared. Every adult had had the vote since 1931 (see universal suffrage in Ceylon), and elected ministers had run home affairs for years. Its leaders bargained politely and backed the war effort. The first prime minister, D. S. Senanayake, got full self-government as a dominion, with Britain keeping its naval and air bases for some years.

The new country was better off than its neighbours, with high literacy, free schooling and good earnings from tea and rubber (see Ceylon tea).

The trouble lay in who counted as the nation. About seven in ten people were Sinhalese, most of them Buddhist. Tamils were the largest minority. In 1948 and 1949 Parliament passed laws that left most of the Tamil estate workers, whose families had come from India in the 19th century, without citizenship or a vote (see Tamil workers on the estates).

In 1956 Sinhala was made the only official language (see the Sinhala Only Act). The country became a republic and took the name Sri Lanka in 1972. The civil war began in 1983.
sum: On 4 February 1948 Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, became independent from Britain after 133 years as a colony. Unlike India the year before, it happened without violence.
